abstract.p: American Indian (AI) adolescents experience disproportionately high rates of substance use, yet the role of substance use and other individual characteristics in friendship network formation within AI-majority reservation schools remains understudied. Most existing research on adolescent networks derives from racially heterogeneous school settings, where substance use is often linked to friendship formation and popularity. This study examines the structural and relational foundations of friendship networks among AI adolescents in their unique cultural context. Using social network data from 9th and 10th-grade students (N = 247) across three schools on a Northern Plains reservation, we employed exponential random graph models (ERGMs) to analyze factors shaping friendship ties. Models assessed endogenous structural processes (reciprocity, transitivity, degree effects) and actor-level characteristics, including demographic factors, substance use (alcohol, tobacco, marijuana), depression, and AI identity. Results indicated that universal structural mechanisms (reciprocity, transitivity) and demographic homophily (gender, grade, sexual orientation) were primary drivers of friendship. However, unlike what is often observed in studies of other adolescent populations, substance use showed no consistent association with sending ties or receiving ties. Similarly, depression and AI identity were not substantively associated with friendship formation. These findings reveal a distinct relational ecology within AI-majority reservation schools, where peer ties are organized around structural and demographic commonalities rather than risky behaviors. These findings challenge assumptions underpinning many network-based prevention programs and underscore the critical need for theories and interventions that are culturally and contextually grounded in the lived experiences of AI youth.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: A substantial body of empirical research has examined adolescent peer networks across various national and cultural contexts, including the United States [1–6], Germany [7], and the Netherlands [8]. Much of this work has focused on schools with racially and ethnically diverse student populations, with particular attention to how race and ethnicity shape friendship formation [6,9–14]. Relevant findings from such diverse settings have informed policies and programs aimed at improving adolescent well-being. However, many schools located on American Indian (AI) reservations serve predominantly AI student bodies, creating a socially homogeneous environment that differs fundamentally from the diversified settings represented in prior literature. Consequently, the dynamics of peer networks within these AI-majority schools remain poorly understood.

Substance use among AI adolescents is a serious public health concern linked to historical trauma, socioeconomic challenges, and ongoing systemic inequities [15,16]. While a handful of studies have examined substance use in relation to social networks using national datasets such as Add Health [13], these analyses subsume AI youth within larger, racially heterogeneous samples. One study that did focus specifically on AI youth network characteristics is Rees, Freng, and Winfree [17], who used Add Health to describe AI networks in heterogeneous school contexts, finding that AI adolescents had fewer reciprocated friendships than White peers. However, their analysis was primarily descriptive and did not model the endogenous network processes examined here. As a result, the specific network mechanisms that may promote or protect against substance use in reservation‑based, AI‑majority schools are not well characterized. Understanding these mechanisms is a critical step toward developing effective, culturally resonant prevention strategies. This paper takes an initial step toward understanding these dynamics by investigating the role of substance use in the formation of friendship ties within AI‑majority schools.

Adolescent friendship and peer networks play a pivotal role in psychosocial development, providing emotional support, shaping identity, and influencing both positive and negative health behaviors [18,19]. Within schools, friendships can serve as conduits for academic collaboration and social belonging, but they may also facilitate the transmission of risky behaviors such as substance use [20,21]. Research in diverse school settings has consistently demonstrated that substance use is linked to friendship ties, often through processes of selection (youth choosing friends with similar behaviors) and influence (friends shaping one another’s conduct) [13,22]. It remains unclear whether these patterns hold in settings where the student population is predominantly AI and where cultural norms surrounding kinship, community, and identity may differently orient relational processes.

This study addresses this gap by collecting and analyzing first-hand social network data from 9th- and 10th-grade students in three schools on a Northern Plains reservation. Using exponential random graph models (ERGMs) [9,23], we examine how demographic attributes, substance use behaviors, depression, and AI identity are associated with friendship formation within these AI-majority educational contexts. By focusing on reservation schools, where AI youth are the norm rather than a statistical minority, this research moves beyond generalizations derived from prior research and contributes new insights into the unique architecture of AI adolescent social worlds.

sec.title: Factors influencing adolescent friendship formation
sec.p: In social network analysis (SNA), friendship nominations from one individual to another are treated as directional ties in the network, and the individual adolescents are viewed as the nodes. Friendship ties can either be outbound (sending or nominating another as a friend) or inbound (receiving a friendship nomination), reflecting the directional nature of these connections. Previous empirical research from non-AI adolescents has found that the formation of friendship ties is influenced by a myriad of factors, broadly categorized into two main groups. First, there are factors that derive from the network structure itself, known as endogenous factors, such as reciprocity, transitivity, and degree-related effects. Second, there are factors based on the attributes of the individuals, referred to as actor-based characteristics. Actor-based characteristics can be further broken down into three types: sender effects, receiver effects, and homophily effects. These effects are explained in more detail below.

sec.title: Endogenous factors
sec.p: Social networks tend to form characteristic structural patterns, wherein the existence of certain ties influences the formation of others. These patterns, associated with endogenous factors, arise from the relational architecture of the network itself and are fundamental to understanding social system dynamics [2,24]. Key endogenous mechanisms include reciprocity, transitivity, and degree-related effects. Critically, their prevalence and strength are not culturally neutral but are shaped by the social norms and relational expectations of a community [25]. In AI reservation schools, cultural values emphasizing kinship, collectivism, and community interdependence provide a distinct social context that likely shapes these endogenous network processes, fostering a cohesive relational fabric among adolescents [26].

Reciprocity refers to the mutual exchange and acknowledgement of social ties, observed through reciprocated friendship nominations. It is a cornerstone of relational trust and a fundamental norm in adolescent peer groups [2,4]. In AI communities, principles of reciprocity are deeply embedded in cultural teachings, kinship systems, and a framework of mutual obligation that supports collective well-being [26,27]. This cultural foundation translates the structural tendency for reciprocity into a normative expectation within social conduct, suggesting that reciprocal friendships may be especially pronounced in AI adolescent networks [4].

Transitivity and two‑path effects. Transitivity, or triadic closure, is the likelihood that two individuals become friends if they share a mutual friend, serving as a primary driver of clustering and subgroup formation [9,10]. This “friend of a friend” dynamic fosters cohesive peer environments. In close‑knit AI communities, social worlds often deeply overlap across familial, school, and communal activities, creating abundant opportunities for triadic closure [9]. However, transitivity necessarily builds upon open two‑step sequences (i.e., two‑paths), where one person is indirectly connected to another through an intermediary. To distinguish the tendency to form such open indirect ties from the tendency to close them into triads, we also account for two‑path effects [28]. Including both terms allows the transitivity effect to reflect closure beyond what would be expected from the baseline presence of two‑step paths. Consequently, transitivity is expected to be a significant structural force within these networks, reinforced by a culturally rooted context of high community cohesion and interconnected social spheres and we expect this tendency toward closure to be at least as strong as—and plausibly stronger than—that documented in less cohesive school settings, given the dense overlap of familial, school, and communal social spheres.

Degree-related effects capture patterns in the distribution of friendship ties, such as preferential attachment (where popular individuals attract more ties) or constraints on popularity [29]. Prior findings in general adolescent populations are mixed, showing evidence for both preferential attachment and popularity saturation [2,5]. In AI communities, cultural values often emphasize egalitarianism and collective well-being over individual status [27]. This cultural context may constrain the formation of overt popularity hierarchies, leading to more dispersed tie distributions and moderating the effect of preferential attachment [5]. We therefore explore the nature of degree effects, whether they indicate preferential attachment or egalitarian constraints, within these specific AI adolescent contexts.

sec.title: Individual’s characteristics
sec.p: Beyond structural network forces, individual attributes shape friendship ties through sender effects (how attributes influence the propensity to initiate nominations), receiver effects (how attributes affect the likelihood of being nominated), and homophily (the tendency to form ties with similar others) [30]. We examine each attribute systematically, first summarizing evidence from non-AI adolescent populations and then articulating how the cultural context of AI-majority reservation schools may alter these patterns.

Substance use. In racially heterogeneous schools, substance use—alcohol, tobacco, and marijuana—consistently predicts friendship dynamics. Adolescents who use substances tend to receive more friendship nominations (positive receiver effects) [13], and homophily on substance use is well documented: youth are more likely to befriend peers with similar consumption patterns [11,22]. These patterns reflect a social ecology in which risky behaviors confer status and serve as a basis for peer identification in diverse, often anonymizing school environments [20].

However, the cultural context of AI reservation communities may fundamentally attenuate these effects. Cultural frameworks emphasizing communal well-being, collective responsibility, and egalitarianism de-emphasize individual status competition [26,27]. In settings where kinship obligations and community health are prioritized, substance use may not operate as a socially rewarded signal; rather, it may be understood through lenses of historical trauma and systemic marginalization rather than personal deviance [15]. Consequently, we expect that substance use will show weaker sender, receiver, and homophily effects in AI-majority schools than observed in heterogeneous populations. sec.p: Depression. Prior research in general adolescent populations links depression to friendship dynamics through several distinct network-selection mechanisms, and the evidence does not point to a single dominant pathway. Depressed youth often receive fewer friendship nominations (negative receiver effects), but this pattern is consistent with multiple processes, including peer avoidance of depressed adolescents, withdrawal by depressed adolescents themselves, and depression homophily—the tendency of depressed youth to select one another as friends. For example, Schaefer, Kornienko, and Fox (2011) show that depression homophily can emerge from withdrawal by depressed egos rather than from avoidance by alters [31]. Sender effects, meanwhile, are inconsistent across studies.

Within AI communities, the stigma attached to psychological distress may operate differently. Shared experiences of historical trauma and culturally grounded understandings of suffering may foster greater social tolerance toward depressive symptoms [27]. Depression may thus be less predictive of peer rejection in AI-majority settings than in heterogeneous schools where individual competitiveness and overt emotional expression shape peer evaluations. We therefore examine which of these mechanisms—receiver effects, withdrawal-related sender effects, or homophily—operate in AI-majority school contexts.

AI identity. A theoretically important yet understudied attribute is the strength of adolescents’ identification with their AI heritage. Identity affirmation—positive feelings of belonging, pride, and commitment to one’s AI group—has been linked to resilience and psychological well-being in Indigenous youth [37], but its role in friendship network formation has not been examined.

We include AI identity for two reasons. First, in contexts where Indigenous identity has been historically suppressed, high identity affirmation may signal cultural engagement and serve as a marker of shared values and practices, potentially increasing the likelihood of receiving friendship nominations (positive receiver effect). Second, in an AI-majority school, nearly all students share the same racial category; variation in strength of identity affirmation may therefore become a salient dimension of differentiation. Youth with stronger AI identity may be more embedded in kinship and community networks, making identity affirmation a basis for homophilous attraction. Alternatively, because AI identity is largely shared in this population, its predictive power for tie formation may be limited. Given the exploratory nature of this investigation, we do not formulate directional hypotheses but examine sender, receiver, and homophily effects empirically.

Demographics. We also include gender, grade, and sexual orientation, which play two roles in our analysis. Substantively, gender and grade homophily are among the most robust findings in adolescent network research [9, 12]; we expect these patterns to replicate in AI-majority schools, where gender- and grade-segregated activities similarly organize peer interaction. These replicated patterns serve as a comparative baseline against which the more culturally variable attributes (substance use, depression, and AI identity) can be interpreted. Sexual orientation homophily has received limited attention in the literature, but documented social stratification along sexual identity lines in adolescent populations suggests that it may likewise structure friendship ties [9]. Methodologically, the demographic sender and receiver terms additionally serve as adjustment variables that account for demographic sorting in friendship nominations, so that the focal attribute effects can be interpreted net of these compositional forces. We return to this adjustment logic in the Measures section.

Table 1 provides a summary of prior findings for each of these attributes, organized by mechanism (sender, receiver, homophily), drawn from studies of predominantly non-AI adolescent samples. These benchmarks enable a structured interpretation of whether observed patterns in AI-majority reservation schools align with or diverge from established trends.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: In our study, we established partnerships with three schools on a large Northern Plains reservation to conduct a comprehensive cross-sectional social network survey among 9th- and 10th-grade students. The schools were purposefully selected to represent a broad spectrum of social environments on the reservation. Our selection included a tribal school in one of the most geographically isolated and smallest villages (school A), another larger tribal school in a more populous village (school B), and a private, college preparatory school situated near the largest village in the area (school C). We had an overall response rate of 77% across the three schools. Specifically, 72% of eligible students completed surveys in School A (n = 52 out of 72), 76% in School B (n = 140 out of 184), and 84% in School C (n = 71 out of 84), for a total sample size of 263. This strategic choice of diverse educational settings was crucial for exploring variation within the reservation’s social networks. Moreover, it provides a basis for indirect comparison with patterns reported in prior non-AI studies. This comparative aspect is vital for a deeper understanding of the unique social network characteristics in AI communities, particularly in educational and adolescent contexts.

sec.title: 1. Survey instrument and data collection
sec.p: The survey consisted of two primary sections: the first collected demographic information, measures of AI identity, depression, and substance use; the second collected directed friendship nominations. We used Network Canvas, a software platform designed for collecting social network data [32]. All measures were reviewed for cultural appropriateness and relevance by a Community Advisory Board and a Youth Advisory Board from the participating communities prior to finalization [33].

Trained research team members administered the survey during school hours. Students provided responses directly on tablets. Written informed assent was obtained digitally from all participants, with hard copies provided afterward. For students under 18, passive parental permission procedures were utilized. The study was approved by the Colorado Multiple Institutional Review Board (COMIRB #20–2867) and the Tribal Research Review Board. All participants received a $25 gift card upon completion.

sec.title: 2. Missing data
sec.p: Of the 247 participants with complete network data, item non-response was limited to the substance use variables. Specifically, 16 participants (6.5%) selected ‘Refuse to answer’ for alcohol use, 14 (5.7%) for tobacco use, and 21 (8.5%) for marijuana use. For these cases, we utilized available peer perception data to infer behavior. Participants were asked to nominate up to 10 closest friends and then answer questions about each nominated peer’s behavior, including: ‘In the past year, how often has this person drunk alcohol (more than a sip)?’ Response options ranged from 0 (never) to 5 (daily). If over half of a respondent’s incoming friendship nominations (i.e., peers who had nominated them as a friend) indicated peer perception of them engaging in a specific substance use behavior (response ≥ 2, corresponding to ‘a few times a year’ or more), the respondent was classified as a user (1) for that variable; otherwise, they were classified as a non-user (0). This approach leverages the insight that peers often have accurate knowledge of each other’s substance use behaviors, particularly in small, close-knit school environments where social information diffuses rapidly through friendship networks [21]. To confirm the robustness of this approach, we compared the primary models with models excluding these cases; the direction of every focal effect is unchanged and no substantive conclusion is reversed (Supporting Information, Table S3 in S1 File). No other key variables (depression, AI identity, demographic information, or friendship nominations) had missing data.

We acknowledge two potential limitations of this imputation approach. First, adolescents’ perceptions of friends’ substance use can be systematically biased, including in the direction of false consensus, in which adolescents overestimate friends’ engagement in behaviors they themselves perform—and perceived friend use may diverge from friends’ own self-reports [34]. Second, because the peers providing the perceptions are themselves embedded in the friendship network, imputed values could in principle introduce or amplify apparent behavioral similarity among connected adolescents, if peer perceptions are shaped by reporters’ own behavior or by friendship-group norms. Two considerations mitigate these concerns. The imputed cases are few (6.5% for alcohol, 5.7% for tobacco, and 8.5% for marijuana), and sensitivity analyses that exclude these cases entirely leave the direction of every focal effect unchanged and reverse no substantive conclusion, although a small number of coefficients—concentrated in School B, where the excluded cases are most numerous—cross conventional significance thresholds, consistent with the reduced sample size (Supporting Information, Table S3 in S1 File).

sec.title: Dependent Variable.
sec.p: The dependent variable was the directed friendship network within each school. Students were asked to “select up to 10 friends you are closest with in grades 7th-12th at your school.” School rosters within the Network Canvas software assisted identification. For analysis, we focused on ties among responding 9th- and 10th-grade students, stored in a square adjacency matrix for each school.

sec.title: Endogenous Factors.
sec.p: We included standard parameters to account for structural network dependence: reciprocity (mutual ties), transitivity (modeled via the geometrically weighted edgewise shared partner, GWESP, term), and the distribution of incoming and outgoing ties (modeled via geometrically weighted indegree, GWIDeg, and outdegree, GWODeg, terms) [23,24]. Following Snijders et al. [28], we also included a two‑path term to separate the tendency for open two‑step sequences from triadic closure, thereby allowing the GWESP coefficient to more cleanly capture transitivity. The decay parameter for all geometrically weighted terms was fixed at log(2) = 0.693, a common choice to aid model convergence and interpretation.

sec.title: Individual’s characteristics.
sec.p: Substance Use Variables: Participants’ use of alcohol, tobacco, and marijuana was measured through binary variables (yes = 1; no = 0), derived from self-reported data in the survey’s initial section. These data are collected through the questions including: “Have you ever had a drink (more than a sip) of alcohol, such as beer, wine, or hard liquor like vodka?”, “Have you ever smoked a cigarette? (Do not include ceremonial use of tobacco.)”, and “Have you ever used marijuana (also called weed, pot, chronic, or nug, including edibles)?”

Depression Assessment: The survey also included a measure of depression, utilizing the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D) [35–38]. This section of the survey consisted of six questions, each probing different facets of depression, such as persistent sadness, feelings of failure, loneliness, and the occurrence of crying spells. Respondents were asked to indicate the frequency of these symptoms using a scale ranging from 0 (rarely) to 3 (most or all of the time).

AI Identity: The measurement of AI identity was assessed using six items adapted from the Affirmation and Belonging subscale of the Multigroup Ethnic Identity Measure (MEIM) [39]. The MEIM provides a validated framework for assessing core, cross-group dimensions of ethnic identity, such as positive group attachment, belonging, and pride, allowing for meaningful measurement across diverse populations. For cultural relevance and specificity within this tribal community, item wording was adapted in partnership with the study’s Community and Youth Advisory Boards, with generic references to “TRIBE” replaced by the specific tribal identifier. Participants indicated their level of agreement on a 4-point Likert scale (0 = strongly disagree to 3 = strongly agree) with statements that included: “I feel a connection with other [TRIBE] people,” “I often think about the fact that I am [TRIBE],” “I think that [TRIBE] people have a lot to be proud of,” “I feel committed to [TRIBE] people,” “Being [TRIBE] makes me happy,” and “Being [TRIBE] is an important part of how I see myself.” An average score across these six items was computed to represent overall AI identity affirmation. The adapted scale demonstrated good internal consistency in the present sample (Cronbach’s α = 0.722).

Demographic Information: Three basic demographic measures were included in the model: grade, gender, and sexual orientation. The information about each respondent’s grade level was obtained based on school rosters provided by the participating schools. For this study, we are only analyzing friendship ties among students in 9th and 10th grade. Respondent gender was gathered via the survey question: “How do you identify your gender identity (check all that apply)?”. Options to select included Male, Female, Transgender, Cisgender (i.e., not transgender), Nonbinary/genderqueer, Agender, Two-Spirit, and Other. Since respondents could have chosen more than one option for the gender question, we processed gender information by male (if male is one of the selected options), female (if female is one of the selected options), and other (if male and female are not in the selected options). Sexual orientation was obtained by asking “How do you describe your sexual orientation?” Response options included Straight, Two-Spirit, Asexual/Demisexual, Gay/Lesbian, Bisexual/Pansexual/Omnisexual, and Questioning. Given the low prevalence of responses outside of the straight category, and to simplify the model, we categorized sexual orientation as straight and non-straight.

These demographic variables enter the model in two capacities. As noted in the Introduction, the homophily terms capture substantively meaningful patterns of friendship formation along demographic lines, which we report and interpret as replication benchmarks. As adjustment variables, gender, grade, and sexual orientation are plausibly associated both with the focal attributes and with friendship tie formation: substance use and depressive symptoms vary by gender and grade during adolescence [15,40], and friendship nominations are strongly structured by gender and grade [9,12]. Omitting these variables could therefore bias the estimated sender, receiver, and homophily effects of the focal attributes. At the same time, consistent with the “Table 2 fallacy” critique [41], we caution against interpreting the demographic coefficients as independent causal effects of demographics on tie formation: the adjustment set was chosen to support the interpretation of the focal predictors, and a single adjustment set is not generally appropriate for estimating every coefficient in the model. We therefore report the demographic terms as descriptive patterns and robustness benchmarks, and we center our substantive interpretation on the focal attributes.

sec.title: 4. Model
sec.p: We employed Exponential Random Graph Models (ERGMs) to model the probability of friendship tie formation within each school, accounting for the inherent interdependence of network observations [9,24]. ERGMs model the log-odds of a tie as a linear function of network statistics representing both structural dependencies (endogenous factors) and actor attributes:

Where y is the observed network, g(y,X) is a vector of network statistics (e.g., counts of reciprocal ties or homophilous pairs), θ is a vector of coefficients, and k(θ) is a normalizing constant. Parameters were estimated using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) maximum likelihood estimation via the ergm package in R [42].

To assess potential multicollinearity among the key independent variables—substance use (alcohol, tobacco, marijuana), depression, and AI identity—we computed Pearson correlation coefficients across the combined sample (see Supporting Information, Table S1 in S1 File). All correlations were modest (|r| < 0.51), indicating that multicollinearity is unlikely to bias the ERGM estimates.

A key challenge in interpreting and comparing ERGM coefficients across different models or contexts is their non-linear scaling, making direct comparison of θ coefficients misleading [43]. To address this and quantify the substantive importance of each factor, we computed Average Marginal Effects (AMEs) using the ergMargins package [44]. AMEs represent the average change in the predicted probability of a tie formation associated with a one-unit change in a predictor variable, holding all other variables constant. This provides an interpretable, population-averaged effect size that is directly comparable across the three school networks [43].

For each school, we estimated a series of ERGMs. This included a base model containing structural terms (reciprocity, transitivity [GWESP], degree distributions [GWIDeg, GWODeg], and a two-path term) and core substantive variables (demographics, depression, AI identity). Subsequently, we estimated separate models for each substance (alcohol, tobacco, marijuana) that added sender (nodeofactor), receiver (nodeifactor), and homophily (nodematch) effects for the specific substance use variable.

From these fitted models, we calculated interpretable AMEs for a balanced set of variables, including key structural parameters and all substantive actor-level variables (e.g., demographic homophily, substance use effects, depression, and AI identity). This approach allowed us to assess not just the statistical significance but the magnitude of each factor’s association with friendship tie probability in each unique school context. Full ERGM results with AMEs for each school are presented in Tables 3.

sec.p: Model estimation and diagnostics. All ERGMs were estimated using Markov Chain Monte Carlo Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MCMLE) via the ergm package (version 4.12.0) in R [42]. Model convergence was assessed using the MCMLE convergence criterion (99% confidence level); all 12 models converged successfully within 25 iterations. MCMC chain mixing was evaluated via trace plots for all 12 models (Figs S13–S24 in S2 File), which showed no evidence of trend or drift. Model degeneracy was assessed by inspecting coefficient estimates for extreme values and MCMC samples for non-finite statistics; no degeneracy was detected in any specification.

Goodness-of-fit was assessed by comparing the observed network to 100 networks simulated from each fitted model (Figs S1–S12 in S2 File): on degree distributions (indegree and outdegree), edgewise and dyadwise shared partner distributions, geodesic distances, and the triad census. In all 12 models, the observed network statistics fell within the central range of simulated distributions, indicating adequate model fit. Full GOF diagnostic plots are provided in Supplementary Materials.

sec.title: Descriptive statistics and network characteristics
sec.p: Table 2 presents descriptive statistics for students across the three schools. School A (n = 49) was the smallest, located in a geographically isolated village; School B (n = 128) was the largest, serving a more populous community; and School C (n = 70) was a private college-preparatory institution. Substance use prevalence varied modestly across schools: marijuana use was most common (37–43%), followed by alcohol (14–24%) and tobacco (16–23%). Depression scores ranged from 4.19 to 4.76 (CES-D total), and AI identity scores ranged from 2.18 to 2.39, reflecting moderate levels of cultural identification.

Basic network characteristics are reported in the lower panel of Table 2. Network densities ranged from 0.026 (School B) to 0.083 (School C), reflecting the low-to-moderate tie density typical of friendship nomination networks where students select from a restricted roster. Reciprocity rates were high across all schools (93.3–97.7%), indicating that mutual friendship nominations were the norm. Mean indegree (friendship nominations received) was 3.43 in School A, 3.27 in School B, and 5.73 in School C, while mean outdegree (nominations sent) matched indegree in each school. Transitivity levels ranged from 31.0% (School B) to 36.5% (School A), suggesting moderate clustering. Notably, School C showed the highest density and mean degree despite having a mid-sized student body, which may reflect the more socially cohesive environment of a residential preparatory school where students interact across multiple contexts. These network characteristics provide important context for interpreting the ERGM results reported below.

sec.title: Endogenous factors
sec.p: The ERGM results revealed strong and consistent endogenous structural effects across all three schools (Table 3). Reciprocity was positive and highly significant in every model, indicating a robust tendency for mutual friendship nominations. Similarly, the positive coefficients for closed triads (transitivity) and negative coefficients for two‑path confirmed that triadic closure—the process by which friends of friends become friends—is a fundamental organizing principle within these AI adolescent networks.

The patterns for degree‑related effects were more varied. The negative and significant coefficients for geometrically weighted outdegree (GWODeg) across all schools indicate a centralized structure in outgoing ties, meaning a subset of adolescents initiated a disproportionately high number of friendship nominations. For incoming ties (indegree), a significant negative coefficient was observed only in School C, indicating a centralized popularity structure in that setting. In Schools A and B, indegree distributions did not deviate significantly from what would be expected by chance. This school‑level variation may reflect differences in school size, institutional environment, or local peer norms regarding status.

sec.title: Individual characteristics and tie formation
sec.p: Substance use demonstrated no consistent or robust association with friendship dynamics in this sample. Sender and receiver effects—indicating whether individuals who use substances are more likely to receive or initiate friendships—were almost entirely non‑significant across all three schools and substances. The only exception was a positive sender effect for alcohol use in School C (AME = 0.015, p < 0.05), suggesting a tendency for alcohol‑using adolescents to initiate more friendship nominations in that setting.

Homophily effects—the tendency for friends to share similar substance use behaviors—were similarly inconsistent. Alcohol use showed significant homophily in School B (AME = 0.0039, p < 0.01) but not in the other schools or for other substances. Marijuana use exhibited homophily in School B (AME = 0.0020, p < 0.10), while tobacco use showed no homophily in any school. Where isolated effects appeared, they did not replicate across schools or substances, underscoring the lack of a consistent pattern.

Depression sender and receiver effects were substantively negligible across all schools; although the sender effect in School B reached statistical significance across model specifications owing to very small standard errors, its magnitude (AME < 0.001) indicates no meaningful association, and AI identity was largely unassociated with sending or receiving ties, with only a borderline positive receiver effect in School C.

Homophily effects provided further evidence of distinct relational logics. Strong and significant homophily was present for gender and grade across all schools, indicating that shared gender identity and grade level are primary axes of friendship formation. Sexual orientation homophily was also significant and positive. Homophily based on AI identity was non-significant, and depression homophily was negligible in magnitude (statistically detectable only in Schools B and C; AME ≤ 0.001).

In summary, the network structure of these AI adolescents is powerfully shaped by universal endogenous processes (reciprocity, transitivity) and demographic commonalities (gender, grade, sexual orientation). Substance use and depression show negligible associations with friendship tie formation within these reservation school contexts, a pattern that diverges notably from prior research on non-AI adolescent populations (see Discussion and Table 1).

To assess whether the absence of substance‑use effects might be due to overcontrol (i.e., the inclusion of depression, AI identity, and demographic covariates), we estimated separate ERGMs containing only structural terms and the substance use variables (alcohol, tobacco, marijuana). The results (see Supporting Information, Table S2 in S1 File) were consistent with the full models: substance use showed no robust or consistent association with sender, receiver, or homophily effects across schools, while the structural processes (reciprocity, transitivity, degree effects) remained significant. This robustness check confirms that the null findings are not an artifact of model specification.

sec.title: Discussion and conclusion
sec.p: This study addressed a gap in adolescent peer network research by collecting original social network data from students in three schools on a Northern Plains reservation. Through the use of exponential random graph models, this study examined how key factors, including substance use, are associated with friendship formation. By understanding how factors well-established in non-AI settings function in the culturally distinct setting of a reservation, this work can begin a conversation around culturally resonant prevention strategies for a population facing elevated substance use risks and historical trauma.

Our analysis focused on endogenous structural factors (reciprocity, transitivity, two-path effects, and degree distributions) and individual characteristics (grade, gender, sexual orientation, depression, AI identity, and substance use).

Endogenous factors assessed in this study align with prior research in direction and relative magnitude, with minor departures noted (Table 1). Reciprocity was strongly positive across all three schools (School A: AME = 0.114, p < 0.001; School B: AME = 0.049, p < 0.001; School C: AME = 0.109, p < 0.001), consistent with the robust reciprocity effects documented in studies of non-AI adolescents [9]. Transitivity (GWESP) was likewise consistently positive (AME = 0.016–0.035, all p < 0.001), reflecting the well-documented tendency for triadic closure in adolescent friendship networks [9,10].

Degree-related effects revealed more nuanced patterns. The negative outdegree coefficients across all schools (AME = −0.060 to −0.019) indicate centralized sending structures, consistent with prior findings that a subset of adolescents initiates disproportionately many ties [2,5]. The variation in indegree effects—significantly negative only in School C (AME = −0.045, p < 0.05), and non-significant in Schools A and B—parallels the mixed findings in the broader literature. Popularity saturation (negative GWIDeg) has been observed in large, diverse schools, whereas smaller or more cohesive settings often show null or positive indegree distributions [2,5]. The absence of centralized popularity in Schools A and B may reflect the stronger operation of egalitarian norms in tribal school settings, where kinship obligations and collective identity constrain overt status hierarchies [27]. Taken together, these findings suggest that while structural endogenous processes are universal, their specific parameters are calibrated by institutional context. These endogenous factors are fundamental principles utilized in social network interventions for adolescent substance use, suggesting a promising direction for AI social network interventions [45].

The absence of consistent substance use effects marks the most striking departure from the broader adolescent network literature. In non-AI samples, substance use homophily and receiver effects are consistently positive and often substantial in magnitude [6,11,13,22] (see Table 1 for a summary of prior findings). By contrast, in our AI-majority sample, substance use showed no consistent sender, receiver, or homophily effects across schools. The only exceptions, alcohol homophily in School B (AME = 0.0039, p < 0.01) and an alcohol sender effect in School C (AME = 0.015, p < 0.05), were isolated and did not replicate across schools or substances. This pattern suggests that substance use operates as a weaker organizing principle for friendship formation in AI reservation schools than in the racially heterogeneous settings that have dominated prior research.

It is important to note that depression likewise showed no substantively meaningful associations with friendship formation among AI adolescents, unlike the negative receiver effects and depression homophily commonly observed in non-AI populations [46]; the isolated statistically significant estimates were negligible in magnitude (AME < 0.001). These findings underscore the cultural and contextual considerations that may lead network formation patterns and factors to be distinct within AI communities.

Homophily effects provided further evidence of distinct relational logics. Gender and grade homophily were consistently significant across all schools (AME = 0.008–0.058, all p < 0.001), indicating that shared gender identity and grade level are primary axes of friendship formation, as extensively documented in the broader adolescent literature [9,12]. Sexual orientation homophily was also significant and positive (AME = 0.002–0.028), an understudied pattern that suggests meaningful social stratification along lines of sexual identity even in these small, relatively homogeneous school settings. In contrast, homophily based on substance use, depression, or AI identity was largely absent.

AI identity homophily was consistently non-significant across all schools. This null finding, while seemingly counterintuitive given the cultural emphasis on tribal belonging, is consistent with several contextual considerations. First, in AI-majority schools, racial identity is a near-universal attribute; with nearly all students identifying as AI, there is insufficient variation in racial category for identity to differentiate friendship choices. Homophily on AI identity is theoretically redundant when almost all potential friends share the same racial background. Second, variation in the strength of identity affirmation (our measured construct) may not correspond to observable social cues that guide friendship decisions among adolescents. While strong AI identity predicts psychosocial well-being and cultural engagement [39], it may not function as a visible status marker or interactional filter in the way that substance use or athletic participation does in other settings. Third, kinship networks and familial relationships—which operate largely outside the school-based friendship system we measured—may be the primary arena where AI identity shapes social ties [27]. The borderline positive receiver effect of AI identity in School C (AME = 0.009, p < 0.10) may reflect a subtle status dynamic in the private preparatory school context, where stronger cultural identification could signal embeddedness in community networks valued within a more academically oriented peer culture. Future research should examine whether AI identity effects emerge in more racially heterogeneous school settings, where Indigenous students constitute a minority and identity affirmation may become a more salient basis for in-group solidarity.

School-level variation and contextual mechanisms. The three schools in this study differed along dimensions that may illuminate why certain network processes appeared in one setting but not others. School A was a small tribal school (n = 52) in a geographically isolated village; School B was a larger tribal school (n = 140) in a more populous community; and School C was a private college-preparatory institution (n = 71) near the reservation’s largest settlement. These contextual differences map onto observed variation in network patterns in theoretically meaningful ways.

Most notably, School C was the only setting where incoming ties were significantly centralized (negative GWIDeg), indicating a pronounced popularity hierarchy in which a small subset of students received disproportionately many nominations. This pattern is consistent with the institutional character of a private preparatory school, where competitive academic environments and structured status markers may amplify peer-evaluative dynamics that produce stratified popularity structures [29]. School C also showed a significant positive sender effect for alcohol use, the only such effect across all schools and substances, suggesting that in this more status-conscious environment, alcohol-using adolescents may be more inclined to initiate friendship ties, a pattern consistent with the social signaling dynamics observed in heterogeneous non-AI schools [13].

In contrast, Schools A and B showed no evidence of centralized popularity structures. The absence of significant indegree effects in these tribal school settings may reflect the stronger operation of egalitarian norms characteristic of close-knit Indigenous communities [27], where kinship obligations and collective identity constrain the emergence of overt status hierarchies. The smaller size of School A may further reinforce this pattern, as intimate social environments leave less room for anonymity-based status competition.

Substance use homophily was detected only in School B (alcohol: AME = 0.0039, p < 0.01; marijuana: AME = 0.0020, p < 0.10), the largest of the three schools. This finding aligns with research suggesting that homophily on deviant behaviors becomes more salient as school size increases and peer crowds fragment into differentiated subgroups [1]. In smaller settings like Schools A and C, the limited pool of potential friends and stronger community oversight may reduce opportunities for substance-based peer clustering. The small negative depression homophily estimates in Schools B and C (both AME ≤ 0.001 in magnitude) similarly point to size-dependent social differentiation: in larger peer environments, psychological distress may become a more salient basis for social distance, whereas in smaller communities, shared experiences of hardship may attenuate such effects.

Taken together, these patterns suggest that network processes in AI-majority schools are not uniform but are shaped by institutional context—school size, organizational type, and the strength of community embeddedness. This heterogeneity carries practical implications: network-based interventions for substance use prevention may need to be calibrated to school-specific relational ecologies rather than applied uniformly across reservation settings.

In the realm of adolescent social network research, the correlation between substance use and friendship formation is well-documented. Non-AI researchers have used the recurring connection between substance use and friendship formation as a basis for intervention research with promising results [47]. Our study’s finding that substance use is not associated with relational patterns among 9th and 10th-grade AI youth marks a significant departure from established trends, offering a novel perspective. This finding not only underscores a fundamental lack of theoretical understanding regarding developmental relationship patterns within this demographic but also signals the urgent need to explore more deeply the factors influencing relational dynamics among AI youth. Because the conventional assumption in much of the adolescent health literature, that risky behavior is a primary determinant of relationships in youth, does not hold in our study, which may also mean that common network intervention strategies aimed at reducing substance use may not be as effective as previously thought [4,5,10]. The prevalent approach to adolescent social network interventions for substance use prevention often hinges on the presumption that friendship ties are, to some extent, founded on substance use behaviors. Given that this assumption does not align with our findings, it becomes imperative to investigate culturally relevant alternatives to understanding of how substance use relates to friendship formation. Gaining insight into these alternative predictors is crucial for developing innovative, effective strategies for substance use prevention tailored to AI youth that may center on strengths-based connections rather than social ties rooted in risky behavior.

sec.title: Limitations and future research
sec.p: The findings of this study are not without their limitations. First, we recognize that the results presented here represent only three schools on one reservation. The history, policies, geography, and culture of this reservation all intersect with network formation and maintenance patterns. Our findings may not extend to AI youth in racially heterogeneous schools, where Rees, Freng, and Winfree [17] observed different network characteristics. Future research should compare network processes across majority‑AI and integrated school contexts. While a comparison sample of non‑AI schools would strengthen generalizability, identifying a suitable dataset with comparable schools (similar size, rural location, and contemporary data) was not feasible. Moreover, the unique cultural and contextual characteristics of reservation‑based AI‑majority schools are not readily matched in existing national datasets. Therefore, we focus on providing a detailed description of network processes within this specific, understudied context, recognizing that future research is needed to assess whether these patterns differ across settings. Furthermore, we acknowledge that these data reflect only one developmental epoch of adolescents at one time point. Relational patterns among AI youth will likely differ across the life course, especially in the formative adolescent years that are not captured here.

The literature highlights the role that school transitions (elementary to middle to high school) play in adolescent networks, but our cross-sectional design imposes a fundamental interpretive limit: a single, simultaneous observation of the network and of individual attributes cannot capture changes in network formation and behavior over time. More importantly, cross-sectional ERGMs cannot analytically distinguish selection processes—adolescents choosing friends with similar attributes—from influence processes—friends becoming more similar to one another over time [4,18,48]. Accordingly, the results reported here should be interpreted as associations between actor attributes and friendship tie formation, not as evidence that substance use, depression, or AI identity causally affect friendship formation, nor as evidence that friendship networks causally shape these attributes. Future research should draw on longitudinal network data among this population—for example, stochastic actor-oriented models—to disentangle selection from influence and to understand how these processes unfold during school transitions. Identifying critical periods of change in network formation and influence would be vital for a better understanding of how and when to tailor preventive network interventions for AI youth. Findings indicating differences in social networks, behaviors, and friendship formation across the three schools also suggest the need to investigate how community contexts influence these factors. This study also highlights a significant divergence from other adolescent substance use social network studies and suggests the need to explore strength-based characteristics that may foster network ties as valuable frameworks for substance use prevention for this population. More qualitative research is needed to better understand AI adolescent networks and assess how one can leverage existing patterns of friendship relations in interventions. Lastly, as reservations are sovereign nations and have policies and laws that may differ from the rest of the state, we encourage future research to explore the role of local governance around these issues and the implications they might have on adolescent social network formation and related interventions.

Reviewer #1: Review PLOS ONE: PONE-D-25-35736

This paper investigates the structure of friendship networks among adolescents of native American descent in three schools (263 students in total). The study aims to examine whether network processes characteristic of students without native American descent are different compared to those surveyed in their study. To this end, the authors employ statistical network models and estimate one exponential random graph model for each school. While the goals of the manuscript are intriguing, I have several concerns regarding the theoretical framework and the analysis. I hope my comments are helpful and can serve the authors in further developing their manuscript.
Mismatch between claimed contribution and conducted analyses.

My biggest issue with the manuscript is that the authors claim to study whether network processes differ for Native American students compared to non-Native American students. Yet, all students in their survey are of native American descent; consequently, they can only make rather crude qualitative comparisons with past work, and the generalizability of their findings is very limited. Past work indicated that tie-formation mechanisms differ between contexts according to various characteristics, such as size (McFarland et al. 2014), and that processes connected to racial and ethnic intergroup relations are linked to schools’ demographic composition (Kruse and Kroneberg 2019; Moody 2001; Smith et al. 2016; Zhao 2023).

Hence, drawing overall conclusions regarding tie-formation mechanisms among AI-youth might be difficult without a sample of non-AI-youth students. A potential solution for this issue would be to search for schools in the Add Health dataset or another US-based dataset containing friendship networks among students that are similar in terms of size, racial homogeneity, geographical location (rural area), etc. Ideally, the comparison dataset would be obtained during the last few years to avoid potential time trends in network formation mechanisms. Thereby, the authors could run the same model specifications in these schools and show whether tie-formation mechanisms differ between AI and non-AI schools in a more convincing way.

Currently, the findings overall are showing very similar patterns as other samples (e.g., transitivity, gender homophily, and classroom homophily are present in almost all school friendship networks), and it's not entirely clear to me what the novel contribution of the paper is. The finding that substance use is not predictive of students’ friendship choices, unlike reported in other studies, is interesting, but I don’t think that the authors can conclude from the current analysis that this finding stems from different tie-formation mechanisms among AI-youth. Prior work shows that there is variation in the extent to which substance use structures friendship networks (Gommans et al. 2016; Pearson et al. 2006; Wittek and Xu 2025), and that the authors do not find statistically significant effects could be due to other characteristics of the schools in the sample (e.g., all are located in a rural area, rather small in size, racially homogeneous, etc.). Again, a comparison with similar non-AI schools could help in this regard and enhance the generalizability of the findings. I noticed that there is a study looking at the position of AI-youth in the school networks in the Add Health data that might be highly relevant for the authors: (Rees, Freng, and Winfree, 2014).
Theoretical framework

Another major issue that I see with the manuscript is that the theoretical foundation of the analysis could be much stronger. In particular, it did not become sufficiently clear to me why we should expect that there are differences in tie-formation mechanisms between AI and non-AI youth. Currently, the theory section feels more like a literature review for an explorative analysis, and there are few arguments of why we would expect different network processes for AI-youth. I think the arguments regarding the importance of kinship and community in AI-youth currently mentioned are a good starting point, but they have to be elaborated more and it could be beneficial if the authors derive hypotheses related to specific network processes. For instance, if AI-youth have a strong sense of community and many out-of-school activities in their villages/ a vibrant social life carried by local ties and tradition, wouldn’t we expect that network processes pointing to cohesion, such as transitivity and reciprocity, are stronger in these schools than in similar schools visited by non-AI youth? Qualitative studies on AI-youth (e.g., Peshkin 2013) could be an addition that strengthens the theoretical reasoning as these ethnographies might have descriptions of AI-youth's social life that help the authors to form hypotheses about differences with non-AI youth (see, e.g., Milner 2013).

Another theoretical angle that I felt was underexplored by the authors is the role of AI identity for network formation. There is a range of studies concerned with ethnic identity and friendship choices in European classrooms that highlight the importance of ethnic identity for friendship networks (Leszczensky et al. 2016; Leszczensky and Pink 2019), and these studies might provide some ideas for hypotheses related to AI-identity.
Methods

The ERGMs are solidly executed and the GOF is OK. However, I had a hard time reading the results from the presented plots and would suggest larger plots. Some coefficients are small due to the scaling of specific variables, and it could be a good idea to adjust the axis for these coefficients accordingly. Also, since ERGMs have a non-linear link function, it is non-trivial to compare estimates between contexts, and I would suggest using average marginal effects for this purpose (Duxbury 2019, 2021b, 2021a). Average marginal effects would also allow for a more nuanced comparison of the strength of network effects found in the authors’ dataset with a comparison sample of non-AI youth. Currently, the analysis can only identify whether there is a statistically significant effect or not, but there might be more subtle variations, e.g., a 10% lower Average marginal effect for reciprocity in non-AI youth compared to AI-youth, that are missed by the current analytical strategy. Also, it would be good to report models only including the variables for substance use so that readers can see whether the lack of substance-use-related effects is due to multicollinearity with other effects in the models (for a discussion of the issue of interpreting ERGM coefficients in complex model specifications see, e.g., Martin 2020).
Summary

While I think the efforts of the authors in obtaining this unique dataset and applying network models to it are commendable, I see much room for further improvement of the manuscript. From my perspective, a key adjustment would be to include a comparison sample of non-AI schools with similar properties, estimate average marginal effects in the post estimation to have a stronger generalizability of the findings, and a methodologically more rigorous analytical strategy. Additionally, the theory section could be improved by including more arguments and references that are specific to AI-youths’ social life. Why would we expect different network processes for this population, and how exactly should tie-formation mechanisms differ for AI youth? These questions could be answered more convincingly by the theoretical framework and might also pave the way for further analysis, revealing interesting patterns. I wish the authors good luck with the manuscript and hope that some of my comments are helpful for the research process.

Reviewer #2: General Assessment:

This manuscript represents a valuable contribution to the understudied area of adolescent social networks within American Indian (AI) communities. The study is grounded in a promising and contextually rich dataset, and its focus holds the potential to advance our understanding of network dynamics in culturally specific settings. That said, the manuscript currently lacks argumentative depth in some sections, and additional steps are needed to ensure the robustness and clarity of the reported findings. The comments below are intended to support the authors in strengthening both the conceptual framework and methodological rigor of their work.
Comments:
Formatting:
In-text citations are consistently placed after the punctuation, rather than before it. This should be corrected to align with standard citation formatting practices.
Introduction (Lines 113–146):

While the discussion of endogenous network processes is technically accurate, it reads more like a textbook overview than a targeted theoretical framing. The authors should clearly articulate why these processes are especially relevant or potentially less so in the context of AI communities. Drawing on research about social norms or relational expectations in AI cultural contexts could enrich the interpretation and provide a more tailored analytical framework.

In Lines 114–116, the claim that structural processes occur "independently of individual characteristics or other exogenous factors" omits the role of social norms in shaping such processes (e.g., reciprocity as a norm-driven behaviour, “if someone is kind to me, I am kind in return”). This should be acknowledged and theoretically integrated.
Methods:
The manuscript does not address how missing data were handled. A discussion of the proportion, pattern, and treatment of missing data is essential to assess the validity of the analyses.

In the section “Endogenous Factors” (Lines 245–267), a notable redundancy arises in the description of the structural network parameters. This duplication stems from the earlier section of the introduction (Lines 113–146), where these parameters were already discussed in detail but without a clear connection to the specific research questions..
Measures:

The scale for measuring American Indian identity (Lines 282–289) would benefit from an assessment of psychometric quality, such as internal consistency measures (e.g., Cronbach’s alpha) as it does not seem to be a validated scale.
Results:

Figure 1 is informative. However, to improve interpretability and facilitate use in future meta-analyses, I recommend including supplementary tables that display the full model outputs separately for each school.

Lines 378–408 discuss results in comparison with prior literature during the results section. Such interpretive commentary should be reserved for the discussion section to avoid the impression that the models also provide findings about non-AI populations.
To address potential overcontrol bias in the models, especially given the non-significant findings related to substance use, depression, and AI identity, I suggest two robustness checks:
First, provide a correlation matrix of the core constructs, including these three variables.

Second, if high intercorrelations are observed, consider estimating separate ERGMs for each construct within each school to reduce the risk of suppressor effects or multicollinearity distorting the substantive conclusions.
Discussion:

Lines 411–448 contain references to "previous research" without clearly citing specific studies. Given the detailed referencing in the results section, the paper would benefit from explicitly citing sources here.

The limitations section (Lines 484–480) is relatively brief and lacks a substantive discussion of the implications of the stated limitations. Embedding these limitations within the broader research context would offer a more transparent and critical reflection on the study’s constraints.

Dear Dr. Letina and Reviewers,

Thank you very much for the thoughtful and constructive reviews of our manuscript. We greatly appreciate the time and expertise you have dedicated to evaluating our work. Your comments have been invaluable in helping us strengthen the theoretical framing, clarify the methodological details, and improve the overall clarity of our findings. We have carefully addressed all points raised in the reviews and the editorial comments. Below we provide a detailed point by point response, outlining the revisions we have made. All changes are highlighted in the marked up version of the manuscript.
Response to Editor (Dr. Srebrenka Letina)
We thank the Editor for summarizing the main areas requiring attention. We have addressed each of the four points as follows:

1. Theoretical background and AI specific hypotheses – We have substantially revised the theoretical section to explicitly link endogenous network processes to the cultural context of American Indian communities. We now discuss how values of kinship, collectivism, and community interdependence may shape reciprocity, transitivity, and degree effects (see “Factors Influencing Adolescent Friendship Formation” and “Endogenous Factors” sections). We have also integrated ethnographic and cultural references (e.g., Walters & Simoni, 2002; Whitbeck et al., 2014) to ground our expectations.

2. Methodological information – We have added a detailed subsection on missing data (Methods: “Missing Data”), including how we handled non response on substance use variables using peer perception and sensitivity analyses. We also report the internal consistency (Cronbach’s α = 0.722) for the adapted AI identity scale and provide a correlation matrix (Table S1) to assess multicollinearity. To improve reproducibility, we now describe the use of Average Marginal Effects (AMEs) for interpreting and comparing coefficients across schools (see “Model” section).

3. Presentation of results – We have restructured the results section for clarity. The endogenous factors are presented first, followed by individual characteristics. Instead of a single complex table, we now present four separate tables (Table 3a–3d) for the base model, alcohol, tobacco, and marijuana models, making the results much more readable. We also moved all cross population comparisons to the Discussion section, reserving the Results section for a purely descriptive account of our own findings.

4. Discussion and limitations – We have expanded the discussion to include more specific citations and a thorough reflection on the limitations, including the absence of a non AI comparison sample, the single reservation focus, and the cross sectional design. We also added a justification for why we did not include a comparison sample (feasibility and cultural uniqueness) and suggested directions for future research (see “Limitations and Future Research”).
Response to Reviewer #1
We are grateful for the reviewer’s insightful comments, which have helped us refine both the theoretical contribution and the analytical rigor of the study.
Comment 1 (Mismatch between claimed contribution and conducted analyses):

The reviewer noted that the original manuscript claimed to compare network processes between AI and non AI youth, but all participants were AI. In response, we have reframed the contribution to focus on describing the unique relational ecology within AI majority reservation schools, rather than making direct comparisons. We acknowledge that our findings may not generalize to other settings and we now cite Rees, Freng, and Winfree (2014) as a relevant study that examined AI youth networks in heterogeneous school contexts. In the Introduction, we clarify that their work was descriptive and did not model endogenous network processes, highlighting the gap our study fills. In the Limitations section, we explain that a direct comparison with non AI schools was not feasible due to the lack of a suitable contemporary dataset that matches the cultural and contextual characteristics of reservation based AI majority schools.
Comment 2 (Theoretical framework):

The reviewer pointed out that the theory section lacked clear expectations for why AI youth networks might differ. We have rewritten the theory sections to incorporate cultural arguments more explicitly. Specifically, we discuss how values of kinship, collectivism, and mutual obligation may strengthen reciprocity and transitivity, and how egalitarian norms may constrain degree centralization. We also added a discussion of the role of AI identity and cultural frameworks in moderating substance use homophily (see “Factors Influencing Adolescent Friendship Formation” and “Endogenous Factors”). We have not formulated formal hypotheses, as the study is exploratory in this understudied context, but we now provide clear rationales for expected patterns.
Comment 3 (Methods – use of average marginal effects and substance only models):

We followed the reviewer’s suggestion and now present Average Marginal Effects (AMEs) alongside the raw coefficients in Tables 3a–3d. The AMEs are interpreted in the text and allow for a more meaningful comparison across schools. In addition, we estimated separate ERGMs containing only structural terms and substance use variables (alcohol, tobacco, marijuana). These models (Table S2) confirm that the absence of substance use effects is not due to overcontrol; the results remain consistent with the full models. We have also added a correlation matrix (Table S1) to show that multicollinearity is not a concern.
Comment 4 (Comparison sample):

We understand the reviewer’s suggestion to include a comparison sample of non AI schools. After careful consideration, we concluded that identifying a suitable dataset with comparable schools (similar size, rural location, and contemporary data) was not feasible. Moreover, the unique cultural and contextual characteristics of reservation based AI majority schools are not readily matched in existing national datasets. We have therefore clarified in the Limitations section that our focus is on providing a detailed description of network processes within this specific, understudied context, and we encourage future research to compare across settings.
Comment 5 (Figure readability and scaling):

The reviewer noted that the coefficient plot was difficult to read. We have removed the figure from the main text (as per the journal’s formatting requirements) and instead present the full results in a series of clearly formatted tables (Tables 3a–3d). We believe this provides a more accessible and comprehensive presentation of the findings.
Response to Reviewer #2
We thank Reviewer #2 for the detailed assessment and constructive suggestions that have greatly improved the manuscript.
Comment 1 (Formatting – citation placement):

We have corrected the citation placement throughout the manuscript. All citations now appear before the punctuation, in accordance with PLOS ONE’s style. We appreciate the reviewer’s attention to this detail.
Comment 2 (Introduction – theoretical framing):

The reviewer noted that the introduction lacked a targeted theoretical framing for AI communities. We have revised the introduction to more explicitly explain why cultural norms of kinship and community interdependence might shape endogenous network processes. We now reference ethnographic work (e.g., Walters & Simoni, 2002; Whitbeck et al., 2014) to ground these arguments. In the “Factors Influencing Adolescent Friendship Formation” section, we also integrate the role of social norms (e.g., reciprocity as a norm driven behavior) to avoid the impression that structural processes operate independently of culture.
Comment 3 (Methods – missing data):

We added a dedicated “Missing Data” subsection (see Methods) that describes the proportion and pattern of missing responses for substance use variables, the peer perception imputation method, and the sensitivity analysis we performed. This addresses the reviewer’s concern about the validity of the analyses.
Comment 4 (Methods – redundancy in endogenous factors description):

The reviewer pointed out that the description of endogenous factors was repeated. We have consolidated the theoretical discussion in the introduction and “Factors Influencing Adolescent Friendship Formation” section, and kept the Methods section concise, focusing only on the specific parameter definitions and model specifications.
Comment 5 (Measures – psychometric quality of AI identity scale):
We now report the internal consistency (Cronbach’s α = 0.722) for the adapted AI identity scale in the “Measures” section. This demonstrates that the scale is reliable in our sample.
Comment 6 (Results – interpretive commentary and supplementary tables):

We have moved all interpretive commentary that compares our findings to prior literature into the Discussion section, leaving the Results section purely descriptive. We have also provided full ERGM outputs in Tables 3a–3d and placed the substance only models (Table S2) in the supplementary materials, as suggested.
Comment 7 (Results – robustness checks for multicollinearity and overcontrol):

We have included a correlation matrix (Table S1) to show that multicollinearity is not a problem. Additionally, we estimated separate ERGMs for each substance without the other covariates (Table S2) and discuss these in the Results section. These analyses confirm that the non significant findings for substance use are robust.
Comment 8 (Discussion – citing specific studies):
We have replaced vague references to “previous research” with explicit citations (e.g., [4,5,10,42,43]) throughout the Discussion, as requested.
Comment 9 (Discussion – limitations):

The limitations section has been expanded to discuss the implications of the single reservation and cross sectional design, the absence of a comparison sample, and the unique cultural context. We also now explicitly cite Rees, Freng, and Winfree (2014) to contextualize the generalizability of our findings. The section now offers a more transparent and critical reflection on the study’s constraints.
Additional Changes
• Funding statement: We have removed the funding information from the manuscript, as per journal requirements. The role of the funders will be provided in the online submission form.

• Ethics statement: We have ensured that the full name of the IRB (Colorado Multiple Institutional Review Board) and the Tribal Research Review Board are included, along with a description of consent procedures.

• Data availability: A data availability statement has been added, noting that due to tribal governance and ethical restrictions, the data cannot be shared publicly. Contact information for the Tribal Research Review Board is provided for any data access inquiries.
• Figure 1: We have removed the figure from the manuscript and now rely on the detailed tables (Tables 3a–3d) to present the ERGM results. The figure is no longer referenced in the text.

We believe that these revisions have substantially strengthened the manuscript and addressed all the concerns raised by the reviewers and the editor. We are very grateful for the opportunity to improve our work and hope that it is now suitable for publication in PLOS ONE.
Thank you again for your time and expertise.
Sincerely,
