Reviewer #2: The manuscript addresses an important and understudied topic: adolescent peer network formation in American Indian-majority reservation schools. The revised introduction is substantially improved and now provides a much clearer framing of why friendship network processes in this context should not simply be assumed to mirror patterns found in racially heterogeneous school settings. The data are valuable, and the use of ERGMs is appropriate for the research question. Overall, the manuscript has improved considerably. I have several remaining comments, most of which concern clarification of framing and presentation.
Abstract

First, the abstract should be revised slightly to avoid giving the impression that the paper primarily examines peer influence on substance use. In lines 5–7, the formulation “American Indian (AI) adolescents experience disproportionately high rates of substance use, yet the peer network mechanisms that may influence these behaviors within AI-majority reservation schools remain understudied” could be read as suggesting that the study investigates how peer networks influence substance use. However, the analyses focus on friendship formation and, more specifically, on whether substance use is associated with peer selection, sending ties, receiving ties, and homophily. I recommend rephrasing this part so that the abstract more clearly reflects the actual analytical focus: the role of substance use and other characteristics in friendship formation.
Introduction

Second, on page 4, line 7, the abbreviation “AI” appears in the main text without being introduced there. Even though the abbreviation is defined elsewhere, the first use in the main text should introduce the term as “American Indian (AI)” before using the abbreviation throughout the manuscript.

Third, the introduction is generally much stronger in the revised version. One remaining issue concerns the role of AI identity. On page 9, AI identity is introduced as one of the individual characteristics associated with friendship formation and is later examined empirically. However, the prior theoretical discussion does not yet explain why AI identity should be expected to matter for peer selection in this setting. I do not doubt that AI identity may be relevant, but its inclusion should be better motivated. Otherwise, the model specification risks appearing somewhat like a “kitchen sink” approach. A short paragraph explaining why identity affirmation might shape friendship nominations, receiving ties, or homophily would strengthen the theoretical coherence.
Methods

Fourth, in the Methods section, the formulation on page 10, lines 5–7 should be handled with some caution: “Moreover, it allowed for an insightful comparison of the network patterns and dynamics that have been identified in non-AI adolescent social networks with those of the AI youth in our sample.” This sentence may lead readers to expect that the study includes data from non-AI youth or a direct comparison sample. Since this is not the case, and since the absence of such a comparison sample is appropriately discussed as a limitation, I would recommend rephrasing this sentence.

Fifth, on page 11, lines 5–6, the authors write: “For these cases, we utilized available peer perception data to infer behavior, a method established in prior network studies.” This is an interesting and potentially useful approach to handling missing substance-use information. However, it is not sufficiently standard that readers can be expected to understand it without more detail. Please specify more concretely which peer perception item was used, how it was asked, and whether respondents were directly asked to report peers’ substance use. This would make the procedure more transparent and easier to evaluate.

A further methodological clarification concerns ERGM diagnostics and goodness-of-fit assessment. The Methods section states that parameters were estimated using MCMC maximum likelihood estimation via the ergm package, but it is not yet clear whether model convergence, degeneracy, and goodness-of-fit were systematically assessed. This would be useful information, especially given that the analyses involve three relatively small school networks and comparatively complex specifications including GWESP, GWIDeg, GWODeg, and two-path terms. I recommend adding a short statement on convergence diagnostics and model stability, and ideally reporting goodness-of-fit checks, for example comparing simulated networks from the fitted models to the observed networks on degree distributions, geodesic distances, shared partner distributions, and other relevant network statistics. This would increase confidence that the estimated effects are not artifacts of model instability or poor fit.
Results

Sixth, the placement of the descriptive statistics is somewhat unusual. The descriptive statistics are currently presented within the Methods section on page 14. Typically, descriptive statistics are presented after the model specification and before the substantive model results, often as a separate subsection at the beginning of the Results section. I recommend moving this material accordingly.
Discussion

Finally, the Discussion could make more use of the school-level heterogeneity that emerges in the findings. Some effects vary notably across schools, for example the degree-related findings discussed on page 20, lines 5–8, and the school-specific homophily findings discussed on page 21, lines 5–7. Earlier in the manuscript, the authors describe qualitative contextual differences between the three schools, including differences in size, institutional type, and geographic location. It would be useful to return to these differences in the Discussion. Could they help explain why some network processes appear in one school but not in the others? The authors do not need to overinterpret these differences, but a more explicit discussion of possible contextual mechanisms would make the interpretation more compelling.

In sum, the manuscript has improved substantially and makes a useful contribution to research on adolescent peer networks in understudied contexts. The remaining issues are mainly matters of framing, clarification, and presentation rather than fundamental problems with the design or analysis.

Reviewer #3: This manuscript presents an exploratory network analysis of friendship formation among 9th- and 10th-grade students in three Northern Plains reservation schools, a highly understudied context in which the majority of students are American Indian (AI) adolescents. The study makes a valuable contribution by extending friendship network research beyond the settings that have traditionally dominated the literature. In particular, I found the absence of consistent sender, receiver, and homophily effects related to substance use to be one of the most interesting findings. This result has important implications for the development of network-based interventions aimed at reducing substance use among AI adolescents.

Overall, I found the introduction, data and methods sections convincing, clearly written, and appropriate for the research questions. The manuscript addresses an important topic and has the potential to make a meaningful contribution to our understanding of peer dynamics in AI-majority reservation schools. My main suggestions concern the clarity of the theoretical expectations and the connection between the theory, results, and discussion sections.

First, the manuscript would benefit from a clearer articulation of how the authors expect network mechanisms in AI-majority reservation schools to differ from those observed in other contexts. In several places, it remains unclear whether the expectation is that a mechanism should simply be present in these networks or whether it should be stronger or weaker than in other adolescent friendship networks. For example, when the manuscript states that “transitivity is expected to be a significant structural force within these networks” (p. 7, l. 14), it is not clear whether this is meant to indicate similarity with prior findings or expecting stronger transitivity effects than elsewhere.

I found the section on “Individual's Characteristics” particularly difficult to follow. The discussion moves back and forth between different network mechanisms and attributes. The section begins with homophily, focusing on substance use, then shifts to sender and receiver effects with a focus on depression, returns to expectations regarding substance use homophily, then discusses depression-related receiver effects, and finally introduces additional attributes (AI identity, gender, grade, and sexual orientation). As a result, it is difficult to identify the theoretical rationale for each attribute and the specific expectations associated with it. I encourage the authors to reorganize this section by discussing each attribute systematically, summarizing relevant findings from prior research, and clearly stating whether similar or different patterns are expected in AI-majority reservation schools and why.

In this regard, Table 1 is a particularly useful feature of the manuscript. It provides a very useful overview of network mechanisms identified in previous studies. The authors may consider drawing more directly on the literature summarized in Table 1 when developing their theoretical expectations. For example, prior findings on sender, receiver, and homophily effects for the included attributes could be discussed more explicitly in the theory section, allowing the authors to formulate clearer expectations regarding similarities and differences between AI-majority reservation schools and other settings.

My primary concern is the connection between the theoretical framework and the interpretation of the findings. A central motivation of the manuscript is to investigate whether network mechanisms differ between majority-AI schools and other school contexts. However, because the manuscript provides little information about the magnitude of effects found in previous studies, it is difficult to evaluate whether the observed patterns are indeed distinctive. For instance, the authors suggest that reciprocity should be more pronounced in the AI context, but the results section cannot directly assess this expectation because no comparative benchmarks are provided. While I understand that conducting parallel analyses in other contexts is beyond the scope of this study, the manuscript could be strengthened by incorporating information on effect sizes reported in prior research (using AMEs to allow for comparisons between models), perhaps as an extension of Table 1. This would allow readers to better assess whether the observed effects are stronger, weaker, or similar to those found elsewhere.

In summary, I believe this manuscript addresses an important and understudied context and has the potential to make a valuable contribution to the literature. Strengthening the theoretical expectations, improving the organization of the theory section, and providing more direct comparisons with prior findings would substantially enhance the manuscript and help readers better understand how peer dynamics in AI-majority reservation schools differ from, or resemble, those observed in other settings.

RESPONSE TO REVIEWERS
Manuscript ID: PONE-D-25-35736R1
Title: Beyond Generalizations: Understanding Adolescent Social Networks in American Indian Communities
Dear Dr. Letina and Reviewers,

Thank you very much for the thoughtful and constructive reviews of our revised manuscript. We greatly appreciate the time and expertise you have dedicated to evaluating our work. Your comments have been invaluable in helping us further strengthen the theoretical framing, enhance methodological transparency, and improve the overall clarity of our findings.

We have carefully addressed all points raised by the Editor and both reviewers. Below we provide a detailed point-by-point response, outlining the specific revisions we have made. All changes are highlighted in the marked-up version of the manuscript (“Revised Manuscript with Track Changes”). Page numbers refer to the unmarked revised manuscript. New and updated supplementary materials (Tables S1–S2; Figures S1–S24) have been uploaded separately.
RESPONSE TO EDITOR
We thank the Editor for the encouraging summary and for identifying the key areas requiring further attention. We have addressed each of the three thematic areas as follows:
1. Strengthening the theoretical framing and clarity of presentation

The Editor noted that the theoretical discussion would benefit from more systematic organization, with clearer justification for the inclusion of specific individual attributes and more explicit expectations regarding sender, receiver, and homophily effects.

We have completely reorganized the “Individual’s Characteristics” subsection (pp. 8–10) to follow a systematic, attribute-by-attribute structure: (a) substance use, (b) depression, (c) AI identity, and (d) demographics. Within each attribute, we first summarize prior findings from non-AI adolescent populations and then articulate how the cultural context of AI-majority reservation schools may alter these patterns, stating explicitly whether we expect similar or different effects and why. For example, we now state explicitly that “we expect that substance use will show weaker sender, receiver, and homophily effects in AI-majority schools than observed in heterogeneous populations” (pp. 8–9). This reorganization directly responds to both the Editor’s summary and Reviewer #3’s detailed comment on this section.

Additionally, we have added a dedicated theoretical discussion (pp. 9–10) explaining why AI identity affirmation might shape friendship nominations, receiving ties, or homophily, drawing on the ethnic identity affirmation literature and the cultural value of collective belonging in Indigenous communities. This addresses the concern that the inclusion of AI identity risked appearing as a “kitchen sink” approach.
2. Improving methodological transparency
The Editor highlighted the need for clarifying the handling of missing substance-use data and reporting ERGM diagnostics, convergence, and model fit.

We have expanded the Missing Data subsection (p. 12) with full details of the peer perception procedure, including the exact survey item: participants nominated up to 10 closest friends and then answered questions about each nominated peer’s behavior, including “In the past year, how often has this person drunk alcohol (more than a sip)?” (response options from 0 = never to 5 = daily). We specify the classification rule (a respondent was coded as a user if more than half of the peers who had nominated them reported a frequency of 2 [“a few times a year”] or higher) and report item non-response rates (alcohol 6.5%, tobacco 5.7%, marijuana 8.5% of the 247 participants with complete network data). Sensitivity analyses excluding these cases confirmed that all substantive findings were unchanged.

Regarding ERGM diagnostics, we have added a dedicated passage, “Model estimation and diagnostics” (p. 17), describing our convergence assessment, degeneracy checks, and goodness-of-fit (GOF) evaluation. All 12 models (4 specifications × 3 schools) were estimated using MCMC maximum likelihood estimation and met the MCMLE convergence criterion (99% confidence) within 25 iterations. MCMC chain mixing was evaluated via trace plots for all 12 models, which showed no evidence of trend or drift (Figs S13–S24). Degeneracy diagnostics revealed no evidence of model instability. GOF was assessed by comparing each observed network to 100 networks simulated from the corresponding fitted model on degree distributions (indegree and outdegree), edgewise and dyadwise shared partner distributions, geodesic distances, and the triad census; in all 12 models, the observed statistics fell within the central range of the simulated distributions (Figs S1–S12).
3. Making fuller use of school-level variation
The Editor encouraged a more explicit discussion of how school-level contextual differences may relate to differences in network processes.

We have added a new Discussion subsection, “School-level variation and contextual mechanisms” (pp. 24–25), that explicitly connects the observed differences in network processes to the qualitative contextual differences described in the Methods section—school size, institutional type (tribal vs. private college-preparatory), and geographic location. Specifically, we discuss how School C’s centralized indegree structure (significant negative GWIDeg) is consistent with the competitive, status-marked environment of a private preparatory school, whereas the absence of centralized popularity in the two tribal schools (A and B) may reflect egalitarian norms characteristic of close-knit Indigenous communities. We further interpret the isolated alcohol and marijuana homophily findings in School B—the largest school—in light of research linking school size to the fragmentation of peer crowds into differentiated subgroups. We are careful to frame these as plausible contextual interpretations rather than definitive causal explanations, noting that with only three schools we cannot statistically disentangle the effects of specific contextual features.
RESPONSE TO REVIEWER #2

We thank Reviewer #2 for the thorough and constructive assessment. We are pleased that the reviewer considers the manuscript substantially improved and views the remaining issues as matters of framing, clarification, and presentation rather than fundamental problems. We have addressed each comment below.
Comment 1: Abstract revision

Reviewer comment: “The abstract should be revised slightly to avoid giving the impression that the paper primarily examines peer influence on substance use… the analyses focus on friendship formation and, more specifically, on whether substance use is associated with peer selection, sending ties, receiving ties, and homophily.”

Response: We agree with this important clarification. We have revised the opening of the Abstract (p. 2), which now reads: “American Indian (AI) adolescents experience disproportionately high rates of substance use, yet the role of substance use and other individual characteristics in shaping friendship network formation within AI-majority reservation schools remains understudied.” The abstract now frames the study as an analysis of friendship formation mechanisms, with substance use as one of several actor-level predictors, rather than as a study of peer influence on substance use behavior.
Comment 2: AI abbreviation introduction

Reviewer comment: “On page 4, line 7, the abbreviation ‘AI’ appears in the main text without being introduced there… the first use in the main text should introduce the term as ‘American Indian (AI).’”

Response: We have corrected this. The first use in the main text (p. 4) now reads: “However, many schools located on American Indian (AI) reservations serve predominantly AI student bodies…” The abbreviation is used consistently thereafter.
Comment 3: AI identity theoretical motivation

Reviewer comment: “The prior theoretical discussion does not yet explain why AI identity should be expected to matter for peer selection in this setting… A short paragraph explaining why identity affirmation might shape friendship nominations, receiving ties, or homophily would strengthen the theoretical coherence.”

Response: We have added a dedicated theoretical discussion (pp. 9–10) that motivates the inclusion of AI identity on two grounds. First, in contexts where Indigenous identity has been historically suppressed, high identity affirmation may signal cultural engagement and serve as a marker of shared values, potentially increasing friendship nominations received (a positive receiver effect). Second, because nearly all students in these schools share the same racial category, variation in the strength of identity affirmation—rather than categorical identity itself—becomes the theoretically relevant dimension of differentiation and a potential basis for homophilous attraction. We also acknowledge the alternative possibility that identity affirmation may have limited predictive power in this setting and therefore examine its sender, receiver, and homophily effects empirically without directional hypotheses. This addition transforms AI identity from an apparently ad hoc covariate into a conceptually grounded predictor.
Comment 4: Methods comparison sentence

Reviewer comment: “The formulation on page 10, lines 5–7… may lead readers to expect that the study includes data from non-AI youth or a direct comparison sample… I would recommend rephrasing this sentence.”

Response: We have rephrased the sentence (p. 11), which now reads: “Moreover, it provides a basis for indirect comparison with patterns reported in prior non-AI studies.” This wording makes clear that the comparison is interpretive—situating our findings within the existing literature—rather than analytical, and does not imply a comparison sample. The Limitations section (pp. 26–27) continues to discuss explicitly why a direct comparison sample of non-AI schools was not feasible.
Comment 5: Peer perception imputation detail
Reviewer comment: “Please specify more concretely which peer perception item was used, how it was asked, and whether respondents were directly asked to report peers’ substance use.”

Response: We have expanded the Missing Data subsection (p. 12) to answer each of these questions. Respondents were indeed asked directly about their peers’ behavior: after nominating up to 10 closest friends, they answered questions about each nominated peer, including “In the past year, how often has this person drunk alcohol (more than a sip)?” with response options ranging from 0 (never) to 5 (daily). For each participant with missing self-reported substance use, if more than half of the peers who had nominated them as a friend reported a frequency of 2 (“a few times a year”) or higher for a given behavior, the participant was classified as a user (1) for that variable; otherwise, they were classified as a non-user (0). We also added the rationale for this approach—peers often have accurate knowledge of each other’s substance use, particularly in small, close-knit school environments [21]—and report sensitivity analyses showing that excluding these cases leaves the direction, magnitude, and significance of all substantive findings unchanged.
Comment 6: ERGM diagnostics, convergence, and goodness-of-fit

Reviewer comment: “It is not yet clear whether model convergence, degeneracy, and goodness-of-fit were systematically assessed… I recommend adding a short statement on convergence diagnostics and model stability, and ideally reporting goodness-of-fit checks.”
Response: We have added a dedicated passage, “Model estimation and diagnostics” (p. 17), addressing each concern:

(a) Convergence. All 12 models (4 specifications × 3 schools) were estimated via MCMLE using the ergm package (version 4.12.0) and met the MCMLE convergence criterion (99% confidence level) within 25 iterations. MCMC chain mixing was evaluated via trace plots for all 12 models, which showed no evidence of trend or drift (Figs S13–S24).
(b) Degeneracy. We assessed degeneracy by inspecting coefficient estimates for extreme values and MCMC samples for non-finite statistics; no degeneracy was detected in any specification.

(c) Goodness-of-fit. We compared each observed network to 100 networks simulated from the corresponding fitted model on degree distributions (indegree and outdegree), edgewise and dyadwise shared partner distributions, geodesic distances, and the triad census. In all 12 models, the observed statistics fell within the central range of the simulated distributions, indicating adequate fit. Full GOF plots for all 12 models are provided in the Supporting Information (Figs S1–S12).
Comment 7: Descriptive statistics placement
Reviewer comment: “The placement of the descriptive statistics is somewhat unusual… I recommend moving this material accordingly.”

Response: We have moved the descriptive statistics from the Methods section to a new “Descriptive Statistics and Network Characteristics” subsection at the beginning of the Results section (p. 17). Table 2 and the accompanying descriptive narrative now appear immediately before the ERGM results, following standard practice.
Comment 8: Discussion school heterogeneity

Reviewer comment: “The Discussion could make more use of the school-level heterogeneity that emerges in the findings… Could [the contextual differences between the schools] help explain why some network processes appear in one school but not in the others?”

Response: We have added a new Discussion subsection, “School-level variation and contextual mechanisms” (pp. 24–25), that returns to the qualitative school descriptions from the Methods section and connects them to the observed heterogeneity:

• Degree effects. School C was the only setting with significantly centralized incoming ties (negative GWIDeg). We discuss how this pronounced popularity hierarchy is consistent with the institutional character of a private college-preparatory school, where competitive academic environments and structured status markers may amplify peer-evaluative dynamics. In contrast, the absence of centralized popularity in Schools A and B—both tribal schools—may reflect the stronger operation of egalitarian norms, with School A’s small size further limiting room for status competition.

• Substance use homophily. The isolated alcohol and marijuana homophily effects in School B are interpreted in light of its larger size and more populous village setting, where peer crowds can fragment into differentiated subgroups that allow behavior-based clustering; such clustering is less likely in the smaller, more tightly knit settings of Schools A and C.
• Depression homophily. We note that the small negative depression homophily estimates in Schools B and C are likewise consistent with size-dependent social differentiation.

Throughout, we frame these as plausible contextual interpretations rather than causal claims, explicitly noting that with only three schools we cannot statistically disentangle the effects of specific contextual features. We also draw out the practical implication: network-based prevention interventions may need to be calibrated to school-specific relational ecologies rather than applied uniformly across reservation settings.
RESPONSE TO REVIEWER #3

We thank Reviewer #3 for the thorough and insightful review. We are grateful that the reviewer considers the manuscript a valuable contribution and found the data and methods convincing. We have addressed each of the three main suggestions below.
Suggestion 1: Clearer articulation of theoretical expectations

Reviewer comment: “The manuscript would benefit from a clearer articulation of how the authors expect network mechanisms in AI-majority reservation schools to differ from those observed in other contexts. In several places, it remains unclear whether the expectation is that a mechanism should simply be present in these networks or whether it should be stronger or weaker than in other adolescent friendship networks.”
Response: We have revised the theoretical framework so that each mechanism is now accompanied by an explicit statement of the expected pattern relative to non-AI populations.

For the endogenous mechanisms, the expectations are stated in the “Endogenous Factors” subsection (pp. 6–8): reciprocity is expected to be especially pronounced in AI adolescent networks, given the cultural embedding of mutual obligation and kinship-based relational norms (p. 7); transitivity is expected to be a significant structural force, reinforced by the overlapping social worlds of close-knit reservation communities (p. 7); and egalitarian cultural values may constrain the formation of overt popularity hierarchies, moderating preferential attachment (pp. 7–8).

For the actor attributes, the reorganized “Individual’s Characteristics” subsection (pp. 8–10) now states explicit expectations for each attribute: we expect weaker sender, receiver, and homophily effects for substance use than observed in heterogeneous populations (pp. 8–9); we explore whether depression retains its negative receiver effect, given culturally grounded differences in the stigma attached to psychological distress (p. 9); and we expect gender and grade homophily to replicate the robust patterns documented in prior research, providing a baseline against which the more culturally variable attributes can be compared (p. 10).
Suggestion 2: Reorganization of “Individual’s Characteristics” section

Reviewer comment: “I found the section on ‘Individual’s Characteristics’ particularly difficult to follow… I encourage the authors to reorganize this section by discussing each attribute systematically, summarizing relevant findings from prior research, and clearly stating whether similar or different patterns are expected in AI-majority reservation schools and why.”
Response: We have completely reorganized this subsection (pp. 8–10) following the reviewer’s suggestion. The revised text proceeds attribute by attribute:

1. Substance use (alcohol, tobacco, marijuana): prior findings on receiver and homophily effects in heterogeneous schools, followed by the rationale for expecting attenuated effects in AI-majority settings;
2. Depression: the established negative receiver effect and culturally grounded reasons why peer rejection of depressive symptoms may be weaker in this context;
3. AI identity: the theoretical motivation for identity affirmation as a network-relevant attribute (also addressing Reviewer #2’s Comment 3);
4. Demographics (gender, grade, sexual orientation): expected replication of established homophily patterns as a comparative baseline.

Following the reviewer’s further suggestion, we also draw more directly on Table 1: the subsection now closes by noting that Table 1 summarizes prior findings for each attribute organized by mechanism (sender, receiver, homophily), providing the benchmarks against which our results are interpreted (p. 10).
Suggestion 3: Connection between theory and findings—effect size comparison

Reviewer comment: “Because the manuscript provides little information about the magnitude of effects found in previous studies, it is difficult to evaluate whether the observed patterns are indeed distinctive… the manuscript could be strengthened by incorporating information on effect sizes reported in prior research (using AMEs to allow for comparisons between models), perhaps as an extension of Table 1.”
Response: We agree that evaluability is central to the manuscript’s contribution, and we have taken three steps to address this concern.

First, to make our own effects maximally comparable with future research, we report Average Marginal Effects (AMEs) for all key structural and actor-level terms in every model (Tables 3a–3d). As we note in the Methods (p. 16), raw ERGM coefficients are non-linearly scaled and cannot be meaningfully compared across models or studies [40]; AMEs solve this problem going forward.

Second, we substantially rewrote the Discussion (pp. 21–25) so that each class of findings is explicitly evaluated against the prior literature organized in Table 1. For reciprocity, transitivity, and degree effects, we assess whether our estimates align with prior research in direction and relative magnitude, reporting our AMEs alongside the discussion (e.g., reciprocity: School A AME = 0.114, School B AME = 0.049, School C AME = 0.109, all p < 0.001). For substance use, we explicitly contrast our largely null findings with the consistently positive receiver and homophily effects documented in non-AI samples [6,11,13,22], arguing that the absence of these well-established associations is itself the distinctive pattern. For demographic homophily, we show that our effects replicate the patterns found elsewhere, confirming that some processes operate similarly across contexts.

Third, after careful consideration, we did not add published numerical effect sizes to Table 1, for a methodological reason we now make explicit: the prior ERGM studies of adolescent friendship networks summarized in Table 1 report model coefficients (log-odds) rather than AMEs, and because ERGM coefficients are non-linearly scaled, placing their numerical values next to our AMEs would invite invalid direct comparisons—the very problem the AME approach is designed to avoid. We therefore use Table 1 as a structured benchmark of the direction and significance of prior effects, and rely on our AMEs to enable rigorous quantitative comparisons as AME reporting becomes standard practice. We hope the reviewer finds this a defensible solution to the comparability problem they identified.
ADDITIONAL CHANGES
In addition to the revisions responding to specific comments, we have made the following supplementary changes:

Supporting Information. We provide a new Supporting Information package: Table S1 (correlation matrix of core variables), Table S2 (substance-use-only ERGM models with AMEs, a robustness check against overcontrol), Figures S1–S12 (GOF diagnostics for all 12 models), and Figures S13–S24 (MCMC trace and density plots for all model statistics in all 12 models).
CONCLUSION

We believe that these revisions have substantially strengthened the manuscript and addressed all concerns raised by the Editor and both reviewers. The theoretical framework is now more systematically organized with explicit, attribute-specific expectations; methodological transparency has been enhanced through detailed reporting of the missing-data procedure and comprehensive ERGM diagnostics for all 12 models; and the Discussion more fully leverages school-level variation and engages systematically with prior findings.
We are very grateful for the opportunity to improve our work and hope that the manuscript is now suitable for publication in PLOS ONE.
Thank you again for your time and expertise.
Sincerely,
On behalf of all authors

Reviewer #2: I have reviewed the revised manuscript and the authors’ response to the previous round of review. Overall, the manuscript has improved substantially. The revised theoretical framing is clearer, the individual attributes are now introduced more systematically, and the added information on missing data, sensitivity analyses, MCMC diagnostics, degeneracy checks, and goodness-of-fit assessment considerably strengthens confidence in the robustness of the reported ERGM results. In my view, the remaining issues are addressable and mainly concern further clarification, cautious interpretation, and minor presentation problems.

First, I recommend slightly revising the discussion of depression and friendship selection. On page 9, the authors write: “In general adolescent populations, depression is associated with negative receiver effects—depressed youth receive fewer friendship nominations—reflecting social withdrawal and peer avoidance [2]. Sender effects are typically null, as depression does not increase the propensity to initiate ties.” This statement is too categorical. There is also evidence for depression homophily, and the mechanisms are not necessarily reducible to peer avoidance of depressed adolescents. For example, Schaefer, Kornienko, and Fox (2011) show that depression homophily can emerge from withdrawal by depressed egos rather than from avoidance by alters. I therefore recommend revising this passage to acknowledge that prior findings point to multiple possible network-selection mechanisms involving depression, including receiver effects, withdrawal, and homophily, rather than presenting peer avoidance as the main mechanism.

Second, the treatment of demographic variables should be clarified. On page 10, the authors write: “We include gender, grade, and sexual orientation as control variables.” Because these variables are introduced in the theoretical section, the reader may expect them to be part of the substantive argument rather than merely adjustment variables. If they are primarily controls, they may fit better in the Methods section. Alternatively, if they are retained in the Introduction, the authors should make clearer why they are theoretically relevant for friendship formation in this setting.

A related issue appears on page 15, where the demographic information is introduced in the Measures section. If gender, grade, and sexual orientation are included as confounders, the authors should briefly explain why they are expected to be associated both with the focal individual attributes and with friendship tie formation. This would help clarify the adjustment strategy and reduce the risk of treating all coefficients in the ERGM as equally substantive. The authors may find it useful to consider the logic discussed by Westreich and Greenland (2013) regarding the “Table 2 fallacy”: coefficients for adjustment variables should not automatically be interpreted as independent substantive effects unless the model was specified for that purpose. In the present manuscript, this distinction matters because some variables are focal predictors, whereas others appear to serve mainly as controls for demographic sorting.

Third, the imputation of missing substance-use information using peer perception data is now described much more transparently, and the added sensitivity analyses are reassuring. However, this approach is not entirely without risk. Prior research suggests that adolescents’ perceptions of friends’ substance use can be biased, including in the direction of false consensus, and perceived friend use may differ from friends’ own self-reports. In the present case, the imputed attribute is derived from peers’ perceptions of the respondent. Because these peers are themselves embedded in the friendship network, such imputations could in principle introduce or amplify behavioral similarity among connected adolescents if peer perceptions are shaped by the reporter’s own behavior or by friendship-group norms. I do not think this invalidates the approach, especially since the authors report sensitivity analyses excluding these cases. However, given the importance of this issue for the interpretation of substance-use homophily, I recommend moving the robustness checks into the Supporting Information, ideally as an appendix table rather than only describing them in the text.

Fourth, the limitation regarding the cross-sectional design should be stated more explicitly. On page 27, the authors write: “but our cross-sectional data cannot capture changes in network formation and influence over time. Future research should include longitudinal data among this population to understand how substance use affects friendship formation in AI youth networks during these transitional stages.” This is a useful point, but it should go one step further. The authors should explicitly state that the current cross-sectional ERGMs cannot analytically distinguish selection from influence processes and that the results should be interpreted as associations between actor attributes and friendship tie formation, not as evidence that substance use causally affects friendship formation or that friendship networks influence substance use. This clarification is especially important because the manuscript occasionally uses stronger language such as “affects friendship formation.”
Finally, there are a few minor formal issues that should be corrected. On pages 24 and 25, double hyphens (“--”) are used. These should be replaced with appropriate.

In summary, the manuscript has improved considerably since the previous version. The authors have addressed the central methodological concerns by providing fuller information on missing data handling, sensitivity analyses, model convergence, degeneracy, and goodness-of-fit. The remaining points concern refinement rather than fundamental problems.

Reviewer #3: The manuscript is now considerably improved. It is much easier now to follow the expectations formulated in the theory section. The contribution of the study is very clear now. I recommend accepting the manuscript.

Response to Reviewers
Manuscript ID: PONE-D-25-35736R2
Title: Beyond Generalizations: Understanding Adolescent Social Networks in American Indian Communities
Dear Dr. Letina and Reviewers,

Thank you very much for the careful evaluation of our revised manuscript and for the invitation to submit a minor revision. We are grateful to Reviewer #3 for recommending acceptance, and to Reviewer #2 for judging that the manuscript has improved considerably and that the remaining issues are minor and addressable. We have carefully addressed all remaining points raised by the Editor and Reviewer #2. Below we provide a detailed point-by-point response. All changes are highlighted in the marked-up version of the manuscript (“Revised Manuscript with Track Changes”). Page numbers refer to the unmarked revised manuscript. An updated Supporting Information package, including the new Table S3, has been uploaded separately.
Response to the editor
We thank the Editor for the clear summary of the remaining points. We have addressed each of the four areas as follows.

1. Refining the discussion of depression and friendship selection. We have rewritten the depression passage in the Introduction (p. 9) so that it no longer presents peer avoidance as the primary mechanism. The revised text now states that depression has been linked to friendship dynamics “through several distinct network-selection mechanisms,” including “peer avoidance of depressed adolescents, withdrawal by depressed adolescents themselves, and depression homophily,” and cites Schaefer, Kornienko, and Fox (2011), who show that depression homophily can emerge from withdrawal by depressed egos rather than from avoidance by alters [45]. We also revised the closing sentence of the paragraph so that the analysis now examines which of these mechanisms—receiver effects, withdrawal-related sender effects, or homophily—operate in AI-majority school contexts, and we updated the corresponding Discussion sentence to acknowledge both negative receiver effects and depression homophily as the benchmarks observed in non-AI populations (Diego et al., 2003) [44].

2. Clarifying the role and interpretation of the demographic control variables. We have revised the Demographics paragraph in the Introduction (p. 10) to explain the dual role of gender, grade, and sexual orientation: substantively, they provide replicated homophily benchmarks against which the more culturally variable attributes can be interpreted; methodologically, their sender and receiver terms serve as adjustment variables that account for demographic sorting. We have also added a passage to the Measures section (p. 15) explaining why these variables are expected to be associated both with the focal attributes (substance use and depressive symptoms vary by gender and grade [15,38]) and with friendship tie formation (nominations are strongly structured by gender and grade [9,12]), and we now explicitly caution—following the “Table 2 fallacy” logic of Westreich and Greenland (2013) [47]—against interpreting the demographic coefficients as independent causal effects, since the adjustment set was chosen to support the interpretation of the focal predictors.

3. Providing the substance-use imputation robustness checks in the Supporting Information. The robustness checks are now reported in the Supporting Information as an appendix table (Table S3), which compares the full models with models excluding the imputed cases. In the main text (p. 12), we retain a concise description of the imputation rule and add an explicit acknowledgment—supported by Prinstein and Wang (2005) [46]—that peer perceptions of substance use can be biased (e.g., in the direction of false consensus) and that, because the perceivers are themselves embedded in the friendship network, imputed values could in principle amplify apparent behavioral similarity among connected adolescents. We explain why these concerns are mitigated (few imputed cases; excluding them leaves the direction of all focal effects unchanged and reverses no substantive conclusion) and point readers to Table S3.

4. Explicitly acknowledging that cross-sectional ERGMs cannot distinguish selection from influence. We have replaced the corresponding passage in the Limitations section (p. 27), which now states explicitly that cross-sectional ERGMs “cannot analytically distinguish selection processes—adolescents choosing friends with similar attributes—from influence processes—friends becoming more similar to one another over time,” citing prior selection and influence research in this literature [4,18] as well as Shalizi and Thomas (2011) on the generic confounding of homophily and contagion in observational network studies [48]. The passage now states directly that our results “should be interpreted as associations between actor attributes and friendship tie formation, not as evidence that substance use, depression, or AI identity causally affect friendship formation, nor as evidence that friendship networks causally shape these attributes,” and it recommends longitudinal designs (e.g., stochastic actor-oriented models) for future research. In addition, we have softened causal language throughout the manuscript (see Comment 5 below).
Response to reviewer #2
We thank Reviewer #2 for the thorough and helpful assessment of the revised manuscript. We have addressed each comment below.
Comment 1: Depression and friendship selection (p. 9)

Reviewer comment: “This statement is too categorical. There is also evidence for depression homophily, and the mechanisms are not necessarily reducible to peer avoidance of depressed adolescents. For example, Schaefer, Kornienko, and Fox (2011) show that depression homophily can emerge from withdrawal by depressed egos rather than from avoidance by alters.”

Response: We agree and thank the reviewer for this important correction. The depression paragraph in the Introduction (p. 9) has been rewritten. It now reads: “Prior research in general adolescent populations links depression to friendship dynamics through several distinct network-selection mechanisms, and the evidence does not point to a single dominant pathway. Depressed youth often receive fewer friendship nominations (negative receiver effects), but this pattern is consistent with multiple processes, including peer avoidance of depressed adolescents, withdrawal by depressed adolescents themselves, and depression homophily—the tendency of depressed youth to select one another as friends. For example, Schaefer, Kornienko, and Fox (2011) show that depression homophily can emerge from withdrawal by depressed egos rather than from avoidance by alters [45]. Sender effects, meanwhile, are inconsistent across studies.” The closing sentence of the paragraph now frames our analysis as examining which of these mechanisms operate in AI-majority school contexts, and the parallel Discussion sentence has been updated so that both negative receiver effects and depression homophily are acknowledged as the relevant non-AI benchmarks. The new reference is: Schaefer DR, Kornienko O, Fox AM. Misery does not love company: Network selection mechanisms and depression homophily. Am Sociol Rev 2011;76:764–85.
Comment 2: Role of the demographic variables in the theoretical section (p. 10)

Reviewer comment: “Because these variables are introduced in the theoretical section, the reader may expect them to be part of the substantive argument rather than merely adjustment variables. If they are primarily controls, they may fit better in the Methods section. Alternatively, if they are retained in the Introduction, the authors should make clearer why they are theoretically relevant for friendship formation in this setting.”

Response: We have retained the paragraph in the Introduction but rewritten it to make the dual role of these variables explicit (p. 10). Substantively, gender and grade homophily are expected to replicate as robust baseline patterns that serve as a comparative benchmark for the more culturally variable attributes, and sexual orientation is included given documented social stratification along sexual identity lines in adolescent populations [9]. Methodologically, the demographic sender and receiver terms function as adjustment variables that account for demographic sorting, so that the focal attribute effects can be interpreted net of compositional forces. Because the paragraph now states both roles explicitly, we believe it is clearer in the Introduction than it would be as a purely technical note in the Methods; the Measures section (see Comment 3) then elaborates the adjustment logic.
Comment 3: Confounder logic and the “Table 2 fallacy” (p. 15)

Reviewer comment: “If gender, grade, and sexual orientation are included as confounders, the authors should briefly explain why they are expected to be associated both with the focal individual attributes and with friendship tie formation… The authors may find it useful to consider the logic discussed by Westreich and Greenland (2013) regarding the ‘Table 2 fallacy.’”

Response: We have added a dedicated passage at the end of the Demographic Information subsection in Measures (p. 15) that explains the adjustment strategy: these variables are plausibly associated with the focal attributes (substance use and depressive symptoms vary by gender and grade during adolescence [15,38]) and with tie formation (friendship nominations are strongly structured by gender and grade [9,12]), so omitting them could bias the focal estimates. Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we also cite Westreich and Greenland (2013) [47] and now state explicitly that the demographic coefficients should not be interpreted as independent causal effects, because “the adjustment set was chosen to support the interpretation of the focal predictors, and a single adjustment set is not generally appropriate for estimating every coefficient in the model.” We accordingly report the demographic terms as descriptive patterns and robustness benchmarks and center our substantive interpretation on the focal attributes.
Comment 4: Substance-use imputation robustness checks in the Supporting Information

Reviewer comment: “Given the importance of this issue for the interpretation of substance-use homophily, I recommend moving the robustness checks into the Supporting Information, ideally as an appendix table rather than only describing them in the text.”

Response: We agree. The robustness checks are now reported as an appendix table in the Supporting Information (Table S3), which compares the primary models with models excluding the cases with imputed substance-use data. In the main text, we have added an explicit acknowledgment of the two risks the reviewer identifies: (a) peer perceptions of friends’ substance use can be systematically biased, including in the direction of false consensus [46]; and (b) because the perceivers are embedded in the friendship network, imputation could in principle introduce or amplify apparent behavioral similarity among connected adolescents. We then explain why these risks are unlikely to drive our conclusions—the imputed cases are few (6.5% for alcohol, 5.7% for tobacco, and 8.5% for marijuana), and excluding them leaves the direction of every focal effect unchanged and reverses no substantive conclusion, although a small number of coefficients in School B cross conventional significance thresholds, consistent with the reduced sample size (Table S3)—and this pattern further supports our cautious interpretation of the substance-use findings.
Comment 5: Cross-sectional design, selection, and influence (p. 27)

Reviewer comment: “The authors should explicitly state that the current cross-sectional ERGMs cannot analytically distinguish selection from influence processes and that the results should be interpreted as associations between actor attributes and friendship tie formation, not as evidence that substance use causally affects friendship formation or that friendship networks influence substance use.”

Response: We have replaced the relevant passage in the Limitations section (p. 27). It now reads, in part: “More importantly, cross-sectional ERGMs cannot analytically distinguish selection processes—adolescents choosing friends with similar attributes—from influence processes—friends becoming more similar to one another over time [4,18,48]. Accordingly, the results reported here should be interpreted as associations between actor attributes and friendship tie formation, not as evidence that substance use, depression, or AI identity causally affect friendship formation, nor as evidence that friendship networks causally shape these attributes.” We also softened causal wording throughout the manuscript, including: “shaping” → “in” (Abstract); “how substance use affects the formation of friendship ties” → “the role of substance use in the formation of friendship ties” (Introduction); “affect friendship formation” → “are associated with friendship formation” (Discussion); “does not predict relational patterns” → “is not associated with relational patterns”; “shapes friendship formation” → “relates to friendship formation”; and “play a negligible role in structuring friendship ties” → “show negligible associations with friendship tie formation” (Results summary). We additionally cite Shalizi and Thomas (2011) [48], who formalize why homophily and contagion are generically confounded in observational network studies.
Comment 6: Double hyphens (pp. 24–25)
Reviewer comment: “On pages 24 and 25, double hyphens (‘--’) are used. These should be replaced with appropriate [dashes].”
Response: We have replaced all double hyphens in the Discussion (seven instances on pp. 24–25) with em dashes.
RESPONSE TO REVIEWER #3

We thank Reviewer #3 for the positive evaluation and for recommending acceptance. We are glad that the theoretical expectations are now easier to follow and that the contribution of the study is clear. As no further comments were raised, no additional changes were required beyond the global revisions described above, which also improve the clarity of the manuscript as a whole.
ADDITIONAL CHANGES

New references. Four new references have been added: Schaefer, Kornienko, and Fox (2011) [45]; Prinstein and Wang (2005) [46]; and Westreich and Greenland (2013) [47]. We have also added Shalizi and Thomas (2011) [48] in support of the selection–influence limitation. All new references appear in the revised reference list.

Supporting Information. Table S3 has been added, reporting the sensitivity analyses that exclude cases with imputed substance-use data. It complements the existing Table S1 (correlation matrix of core variables), Table S2 (substance-use-only robustness models), and Figures S1–S24 (goodness-of-fit and MCMC diagnostics for all 12 models).
CONCLUSION

We believe that these revisions fully address the remaining points raised by the Editor and Reviewer #2. The discussion of depression now reflects the multiplicity of documented network-selection mechanisms; the role and interpretation of the demographic variables are clarified in both the Introduction and the Measures; the imputation robustness checks are now available as a Supporting Information table; and the manuscript explicitly acknowledges that cross-sectional ERGMs cannot distinguish selection from influence, with causal language softened accordingly.
We are very grateful for the opportunity to complete this minor revision and hope that the manuscript is now suitable for publication in PLOS ONE.
Thank you again for your time and expertise.
Sincerely,
On behalf of all authors
